item.title: Fully Forgive and Put Beauty in Relationships and the World
item.description:
Forgiveness

Fully Forgive and Put Beauty in Relationships and the World

Deeper forgiveness allows for mercy and love to pervade relationships.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • If forgiveness is defined as only thoughts and feelings toward offending people, this limits forgiveness.
  • We need a more complete understanding of forgiveness, including behaviors directed toward those who offend.
  • As we deliberately add positive behaviors in our forgiveness of others, surprising issues might arise.

Forgiveness in psychology has been broken down into distinct components, with terms such as "decisional forgiveness" and "emotional forgiveness" (Song and colleagues, 2025). These terms imply that there are forms of forgiveness centered, for example, on particular thoughts, in which the injured person commits to being merciful toward the unfair. Another supposed form of forgiveness centers on particular feelings in which the injured person feels compassion toward the other. In both cases, the "forgiver" can accomplish the entire forgiveness process through thinking, feeling, or both.

Source: Dragoscondrea / Dreamstime

Yet a careful analysis of "decisional" or "emotional forgiveness" shows that they are not only incomplete but also distorted in their understanding of forgiveness as a moral virtue. For example, suppose Jane decides to forgive Martha. Jane can make such a commitment while sitting on the couch, watching soap operas on television, and doing nothing for Martha, ignoring her. As another example, Jane can foster compassion in the heart, and then, that's it. She is feeling better and therefore does not move forward with reaching out to Martha. In both cases, the thinking and feeling components of forgiveness are just that, components and not the full expression of this moral virtue. It is incomplete because, as with all moral virtues, there is a deliberate expression of the good toward others. In the case of forgiveness, this involves goodness toward those who were unjust and even cruel to the person who forgives.

A danger of reducing true forgiveness to thoughts and feelings is that this can lead to a central focus on the self rather than on the offending person. After all, if the "forgiver" decides to forgive and starts to feel better, a conclusion (a false one) could be this: “Well, I am no longer angry or disrupted by what happened. I will let it go now." Notice that this conclusion has a focus on the self, not on the other person. Therefore, this is not an exercise of forgiveness as a genuine moral virtue because, as stated above, all moral virtues entail goodness toward other people. Yet, so often, I read that forgiving others is for the self, to feel better, which can reinforce the idea that forgiveness is an internal process only with a consequence and motivation of helping only the self and not the offending person.

After examining the published philosophical and psychological literature on forgiveness, Song and team (2025, pp. 11-12) defined forgiveness as a genuine moral virtue this way: Forgiveness “includes the motivation (the will) to be good, as an end in and of itself, to the one who acted badly, a decision to forgive, cognitive understanding of this other person as a genuine person, softened affect toward that person, and goodness in the form of behavior toward that person. This includes a reduction in negatives and an increase in positives regarding the variables of thinking, feeling, and behaving toward the other person. This definition is the most compatible with the Aristotelian classical realist perspective."

article continues after advertisement

The Connection Between Fuller Forgiveness and Beauty

Source: Motortion/ Dreamstime

Take a look at forgiving in a fuller sense, when it is not only for the self but also for developing thoughts and feelings within the self. Let us take a broader, less reductionist view and see forgiving as existing for the self and others and taking place within the self (motivations, feelings, and thoughts), but also existing outward, in behavior toward others, particularly toward a person who behaved unjustly. What does this behavior look like? On its highest level, it is argued that forgiving is a reaching out to others, particularly toward the one who acted unfairly, with a sense of what is called agape love, or the kind of love that is in service to others and can be quite effortful and even painful (see Enright, 2012). Agape love is not an isolated phenomenon that exists exclusively within the self and for the self. Instead, it flows outward in the language used toward others and in behaviors that uplift them, helping them be their best selves.

With this view of forgiving as a whole process, rather than just an internal one, we can now see that the definition of forgiving expands to include positive behaviors. This can include agape love. If forgiving includes internal and behavioral transformations that flow from those internal changes, then forgiving can bring more beauty into the world by demonstrating mercy rather than cutting people off, which is too common at present. It can make broken relationships more beautiful because it makes second chances possible. It can make others better by combining forgiving with asking the other to grow in humanity. Forgiveness can bring more beauty to relationships with those who were not the ones who acted unfairly. This can be the case because forgiving can be a preventive against displaced frustration and anger that can tumble onto unsuspecting others. Forgiveness stops the displacement, making room for more wholesome relationships with innocent others, as well as those who offend if they are receptive to the mercy of forgiveness. Forgiveness can bring beauty to communities as people realize that each person there has inherent (built-in) worth, and then act on this realization.

How Can We Practice Forgiveness Behaviors If the Offender Is Gone?

This behavioral issue does not apply only when the offending person is present in your life. You can show positive behaviors indirectly by, for example, saying a kind word about the person to others, or by donating even a small amount of funds to a worthy charitable organization in the person’s name. By engaging in these behaviors, you are putting your cognitive decision into behavioral goodness and exercising your feeling of compassion in a behaviorally constructive way. If the person is still in your life, the behaviors can be even more direct, such as showing kindness and, after forgiving, gently asking the person to change their behavior.

The Science of a More Complete and Accurate Application of Forgiveness

Source: Jason Stitt / Dreamstime

The science of forgiveness therapy, particularly in the context of being traumatized by others, does show, and importantly, that forgiving, when it includes thinking, feeling, and behavior toward the other, can reduce clinical levels of depression (Freedman and Enright, 1996) and clinical levels of anger and anxiety (Yu and colleagues, 2021).

article continues after advertisement

In summary, we must be careful about reductionist definitions of forgiveness that break it down into smaller parts and call them forgiveness. Yes, there are decisional and emotional components of forgiveness, but by themselves, they are incomplete. It is time to see what forgiveness is in its totality, and then develop programs that allow hurting people to forgive more broadly and deeply, and put more beauty in the world.

item.title: Is AI Slop the New Spam?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is AI Slop the New Spam?

How machine-generated language severs thought from prose.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Slop isn't bad writing, it's writing that sounds like thinking without doing it.
  • The phenomenon is old but a new name makes it visible.
  • Repeated exposure may change what we expect thought to look like.
Source: Image by Daniel Agrelo from Pixabay.

You already know what I'm talking about. The essay that brings with it the "theater of thought" but in the end leaves you holding nothing. Simply put, it's fluent but vapid. You couldn't quite complain about it because you couldn't really name it. They drift through the landscape, like wind blowing a piece of garbage.

Let's be honest, this phenomenon is nothing new. Consultants perfected it and academics built careers on it. Marketing and advertising have turned it into a genre. But what's changed is the speed and scale. A machine can now produce it faster than a person can read it. The popular word that captures this is "slop."

In many ways, it's perfect and almost has an appropriate tinge of vulgarity in it. But I couldn't resist adding a bit of structure to the mess.

Superficial
Language
Optimized for
Performance

To me, slop works best as a noun. That's slop. The internet is filled with slop. This feels like slop. And it seems to have a functional and emotional relationship the word spam and how it captured a technological reality.

But what the word actually names is a relationship between language and thought. Slop is writing that has severed the connection between these components, but sounds like it hasn't.

How Slop Differs From Bad Writing

It's important to recognize that slop isn't simply bad writing. Bad writing is clumsy and unfinished and reflects the process of thinking. Slop operates differently. Its output is optimized for the read rather than the idea. Its purpose isn't to explore a thought but to create the experience of having encountered one.

Real thinking leaves evidence of its process. A simple test is to challenge the writer about the prose. Does the response reflect the composition or just result in a cognitive shrug? Slop contains the signals of thought without the event itself. What you get is a structured vocabulary that mimics the cognitive journey. What's missing is the moment where an actual mind met something resistant and had to work its way through.

What Happens When You're Endlessly Exposed to Slop

The danger isn't that slop is wrong as much of it is curiously reasonable. My concern is that repeated exposure can change our calibration for what our thinking looks like. We become accustomed to language that arrives, well, sloppy in this sense. And over time, our own thoughts begins to feel inefficient by comparison.

article continues after advertisement

Naming something doesn't solve a problem, a bit like the introduction of the word "spam." But it does make the problem more tangible. Before you have a word for a phenomenon, you experience it only as a vague dissatisfaction. Afterward, you can point to it, you can discuss it. And perhaps most importantly, you can challenge it.

item.title: Examining the Enduring Appeal Of Astrology
item.description:
Magical Thinking

Examining the Enduring Appeal Of Astrology

Why so many people still turn to the stars for answers.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Astrology shifted from fate prediction to personality analysis in the 20th century for mass appeal.
  • Scientific studies show no evidence linking astrology to personality, compatibility, or events.
  • Even skeptics rate favorable astrological reports as accurate and become more accepting of astrology.

Review of What Science Says About Astrology. By Carlos Orsi. Columbia University Press. 232 pp. $26 (paperback).

In his book City of God, Saint Augustine (354-430) launched an attack on astrology, which had been popular among Greeks, Romans, and Muslims for centuries. “What scope is left to the judgment of God, who is Lord of both stars and men, in relation to the deeds of men,” he asked, “if a celestial necessity is assigned to those deeds?” As Christianity became the established religion in the Roman empire, pagan practices, including astrology, were stigmatized and sometimes punished by death.

Source: Alexas Fotos/Pixabay

Astrology’s Popularity and Modern Appeal

Astrology waxed and waned in the ensuing centuries. In the early 20th century, Carlos Orsi indicates, astrologers pivoted from predictions about the future to “character analysis and psychological counseling,” imparted by the positions of the planets, sun and moon at the precise time of an individual’s birth – and “the queen of pseudoscience” became immensely popular.

Valued at $12.8 billion in 2020, the global astrological market, with its daily horoscopes in newspapers and on computers, and personalized readings by “professionals,” is expected to grow to $22.8 billion by 2030.

In What Science Says About Astrology, Orsi, a journalist, provides a history of the phenomenon, an explanation of its appeal, and an analysis of the harm it does. His book is immensely informative and entertaining.

Orsi supplies a slew of studies demonstrating that astrological emperors and empresses have no clothes. An analysis of ten million couples, for example, revealed no astrological effect on compatibility or incompatibility. Other studies show that people born at the exact same time and in the same locality do not have the same or similar personalities. And horoscopes based on the same birth chart differ dramatically from astrologer to astrologer. Gilding the lily, Orsi points to one well-known astrologer who predicted a year of peace in Europe a few months before World War I broke out: and another who declared that the reign of Queen Elizabeth II would be brief.

Why Astrology Remains Popular Despite Scientific Refutation

Orsi then provides a compelling explanation of the enduring popularity of astrology. Whether a personality analysis comes from a psychologist or an astrologist, he indicates, patients and clients are likely to find something of themselves in it, appreciate a mix of mostly admirable and a few undesirable traits, and embrace their “diagnostics, therapies, and theoretical commitments as valid and useful.” Even subjects who identify themselves as skeptics tend to judge a mostly-favorable report about them as accurate and adopt a more favorable attitude toward astrology.

article continues after advertisement

Experienced astrology professionals, Orsi emphasizes, recognize the importance of their relationship with clients and know how to impress them: appear confident; gear comments to the relevant age, income bracket, education level, race, and gender; listen and observe; elicit information by framing statements as questions; pore over the birth chart; be empathetic and dramatic; tell clients what they want to hear.

Challenging the Therapeutic Value of Astrology

Orsi is deeply skeptical of claims that astrology “can work as a therapeutic ‘myth’ like any other, generating good outcomes in the hands of a competent and empathetic practitioner.” Astrology, he reminds us, has no basis in reality. By downplaying logic, evidence, and critical thinking and relying on arbitrary pronouncements about good or bad hours and days for decisions related to health, love, finances, and professional advancement, the “method” leaves subjects vulnerable to manipulation and delusions they may act upon.

One of “humanity’s longest-lived attempts to make sense of the universe” and find patterns in nature, astrology, Orsi concludes, “belongs now in museums and history books, not in our daily lives.”

item.title: When Behavior Becomes a Cry for Emotional Recognition
item.description:
Child Development

When Behavior Becomes a Cry for Emotional Recognition

Personal Perspective: One child's need for affection revealed the psychology behind disruption.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Children often express emotional pain through behavior before they can explain it.
  • Emotional safety in classrooms can transform behavior and self perception.
  • A caring teacher may become a child's first experience of emotional validation.
Source: edwardeyer / Pexels

There are moments in life that quietly reshape the way we see human beings. Years later, they remain alive in memory because something inside us changed forever. Sebastian was one of those moments in my life.

Many years ago, when I had just started my teaching career in Bogotá, Colombia, I worked as an English teacher in an underprivileged elementary school. I taught English from preschool through fifth grade and served as the class director for a fourth-grade group that many teachers considered difficult because of their behavior. At that stage of my life, I understood teaching through discipline, grammar, and classroom management. I had not yet developed the psychological understanding I later gained through years of studying emotional development, attachment, and human behavior.

Among all my students, there was one boy who immediately stood out. His name was Sebastian.

His shirt collar always looked dirty. His shoes remained untied almost every day. He constantly appeared sweaty, even during the cold mornings of Bogotá. During recess, he ran across the entire school without stopping. He interrupted others, teased classmates, and struggled to remain still inside the classroom. Some children called him “el loco,” the mad boy.

What I remember most clearly, however, was the way he ran toward me every morning.

The moment he saw me entering the school, he would run across the courtyard shouting, “My teacher, my teacher!” Then he would hug me before I even had time to react. At the beginning, I used to push him away gently and say, “Sebastian, you are sweating.” Looking back now, I realize I was seeing the behavior before seeing the child.

During that first month, I noticed positive changes in many of my students. We sang together, spoke about respect, and created routines that gave the classroom warmth. Yet Sebastian remained the same restless child. Beneath all that movement, however, there was something in his eyes that stayed with me. Today I recognize it clearly. I was looking at emotional hunger.

The Hidden Psychological Weight of Childhood Neglect

One evening after returning home, I kept thinking about Sebastian. I remember deciding that the following morning, I would stop stepping away from him.

The next morning, I entered the school and immediately saw him running toward me again.

“My teacher! My teacher!”

article continues after advertisement

This time, instead of moving back, I bent down to his height and opened my arms. Sebastian hugged me tightly and held onto me longer than usual. Then I realized he was crying.

I softly told him, “Everything is OK. I am here.”

Through tears, he replied, “I love you, teacher.”

Without hesitation, I answered, “I love you too, Sebas.”

He slowly pulled away, wiped his tears, and looked directly into my eyes.

“You really love me, teacher?”

“Yes,” I told him. “Very much.”

From that day forward, something changed inside me forever. That was the day I truly became a teacher.

I stopped seeing children as numbers inside a classroom. I started paying attention to emotional regulation, attachment needs, silent distress, and the invisible psychological wounds some children carried into school every morning.

That same day, I decided not to teach English. Instead, I gave my students paper and colors and told them to draw freely. I wanted to understand what existed beneath the behaviors adults constantly criticized.

Over time, I learned more about Sebastian’s life. His father was absent. His mother worked constantly and remained away from home most of the time. He was being raised mainly by his elderly grandmother, who struggled with her own illnesses and limitations. Much of Sebastian’s emotional world existed without consistent emotional attunement or affection.

article continues after advertisement

His behavior suddenly made sense to me.

The noise, movement, touching, and emotional intensity no longer appeared as simple misbehavior. I began understanding them as behavioral manifestations of emotional deprivation and unmet developmental needs.

The Classroom as a Space for Emotional Safety

I later requested permission from the school principal to visit the homes of my students one by one. Over time, I visited all 28 homes.

Those visits changed my life.

I saw poverty, violence, instability, fear, and emotional abandonment. Some children lacked emotional safety even inside their own homes. Several families apologized because they had nothing to offer me to drink. I always smiled and told them water was more than enough.

The children appreciated those visits more than I initially understood. They realized someone cared enough to enter their world without judgment.

From then on, my classes became deeply meaningful. I became aware that these children were not simply students preparing for exams. They were young human beings shaping their identity, emotional development, and understanding of relationships.

Looking back, I now understand that what Sebastian needed was not another behavioral label. He needed emotional attunement, emotional safety, and an adult willing to recognize the child behind the behavior. Research continues to show that children’s sense of belonging and emotional connection within educational environments play an important role in their emotional development and psychological well-being (Bora & Akbaba Altun, 2025).

The hugs that once made me uncomfortable slowly became normal. Other students started following Sebastian’s example every morning. Over time, we created what I jokingly called “hug therapy.” Every morning began with affection, reassurance, and relational safety. Little by little, behavior across the classroom changed. Many students transformed simply because they finally felt emotionally seen and valued.

How One Child Reshaped My Understanding of Human Development

Today, more than 25 years later, I remain in contact with many of those 28 children. They are no longer children now. Some became doctors, nurses, engineers, mechanics, teachers, and taxi drivers. Most built meaningful lives surrounded by people they love.

article continues after advertisement

Sometimes I still think about that morning when Sebastian ran toward me, and I finally opened my arms instead of stepping away.

Years later, while conducting research with offenders and studying the psychological origins of violence, I often found myself thinking about Sebastian. Long before I entered prisons or interviewed offenders, a 9-year-old boy had already taught me one of the most important lessons of my career. Those early observations would later contribute to ideas explored in Dangerous Minds: Psychology of Pain, Crime, and Reparation (Castell Britton, 2025), where I discuss how emotional neglect and unresolved pain can quietly shape identity long before destructive behaviors emerge.

Today, I understand that transformation sometimes begins through recognition. Sometimes through dignity. Sometimes through emotional safety. Sometimes, through one sincere embrace that quietly tells a child, perhaps for the very first time in life, “You matter.”

item.title: The Restless Mind on Stage: Turning Reaction Into Volition
item.description:
Attention

The Restless Mind on Stage: Turning Reaction Into Volition

Internal distractions can be overcome by taming the "monkey mind."

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Stage fright stems from an anxious "monkey mind" dividing focus with judgment.
  • Close monitoring is vital for practicing, but it becomes a distraction on stage.
  • Musicians must practice playing pieces whole, completely focused on the present.
Source: Cottonbro Studios/Pexels

It has been my experience that most issues of performance and practice, including “stage fright,” can be alleviated through the development of sustained and focused attention. Although every person’s experience is different, for many the internal dialogue that takes place while we play can become a distraction during performance. The mind does not efficiently manage multitasking between highly demanding activities, such as accurate performance, and the internal chatter of judgmental observation. The goal for musicians who deal with excessive or pronounced internal chatter is to cultivate the ability to actively choose to focus complete attention on playing, rather than on critical commentary while we are playing.

When we practice, we are in the habit of closely monitoring and examining our playing. Self-observation is a necessary aspect of practicing. This critical reflection helps us to identify areas in our playing that need to be worked out and polished through careful, repeated practice. However, this habit of self-critique also becomes a distraction during performance. When we practice with a high level of self-criticism, the internal judgment becomes a habitual part of our playing. This becomes a distraction during performance and leads to self-conscious fears of things that can go wrong, ultimately robbing us of the mental resources needed for complete absorption in the music.

A way to address this issue is to practice performing. This means consciously changing the practice strategy from addressing technical issues of “learning the piece” to practicing “performing the piece." Practicing performance means playing through the piece, in its entirety, with complete focus on the music in the here and now.

Understanding the "Monkey Mind" and Its Influence on Anxiety

In Eastern philosophy, there is the concept known as the “monkey mind.” Similar to findings in evolutionary psychology, the mind is understood as a restless, craving, sensitive instrument looking for threats in our environment. Individuals who have a heightened sensitivity to perceiving potential threats in the environment are often arrested by the mind’s efforts and become completely absorbed in the mental chatter of “what if!” Gestalt psychotherapy teaches us that anxiety comes from the attempt to control the future, whereas depression is the feeling we experience when attempting to control the past. When we are captivated by the mind’s minding of the potential dangers of the future, or the regrets of the past, we are placing all of our mental resources away from the immediate act of playing in the “here and now."

article continues after advertisement

Training the monkey mind requires a daily practice of remaining in the here and now and gaining volitional control over the seemingly directive monkey mind that is seeking out danger. Some people are surprised to learn that we can take volitional control over what has appeared to be “hard-wired” instinctual mind activity. Through daily, meditative practice, one can cultivate a degree of volitional choice to act rather than react to internal chatter.

The first step in this process is to accept that what seems out of our control is, in fact, a habit that can be reshaped. This is not something that happens overnight; it takes months of rewriting the habitual reactions that we have been practicing since childhood. The effort is not only part of our music making, but it is an overriding quality of our entire way of being in the world, our personality.

Training the mind to sustain presence in the here and now is the point of mindfulness meditation. The techniques of this ancient practice can be learned in a traditional way, through a meditation teacher, or they can be understood in a contemporary psychological and neuroscientific framework, for those who prefer a more scientific framing. Either of these approaches will teach the same habits and can achieve the same results.

Applying Mindfulness to Music Performance Practice

After the initial practice of mindfulness is learned in everyday life, we can begin to apply this to the practice of performance in the music studio. After technical “learning” the new piece has been done, we can devote time in each practice session to practicing our performance of the entire work. Some strategies include closing one’s eyes and pausing before playing, choosing to mentally “center” in the here and now. Feeling the heartbeat of the piece (tempo) and beginning to play with complete focus on beat, tone, and phrase. The goal is to sustain focus in complete absorption into the playing of the piece while choosing to ignore or let go of any thoughts that creep in during performance. Play from beginning to end, for better or worse. This includes playing through memory flubs, recognizing distraction internal dialogue and choosing to ignore it, and redirecting the monkey mind back to pulse, tone, and phrase.

article continues after advertisement

Through the practice of performance, we gain conscious control of what we experience as a natural reaction. We understand that this is a reshapable habit that we can gain volitional control over and that we can enhance not only our playing but our experience of everyday life through the cultivation of staying in the “here and now."

item.title: Cannabis and Nicotine Co-Use Among Youth is Rising
item.description:
Addiction

Cannabis and Nicotine Co-Use Among Youth is Rising

THC and nicotine, increasingly combined, present new addiction and mental health risks.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Cannabis–nicotine co-use is increasingly driven by vaping devices and nicotine pouches rather than cigarettes.
  • Perceived risks of cannabis continue there decline even as perceived harms of tobacco continue to rise.
  • Nicotine and cannabis reinforce one another through shared brain reward pathways, increasing dependence risk.
  • Modern nicotine delivery systems and changing norms have made THC–nicotine co-use common but mostly invisible.

Cigarette smoking among American adolescents has fallen to historic lows, representing one of the most significant public health successes of recent decades. Yet nicotine exposure has not disappeared; it has simply changed form. Today, many youth encounter nicotine through alternative products such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, which supply nicotine orally without requiring the constant spitting associated with traditional smokeless tobacco. While these products may reduce many harms associated with combustible cigarettes, they can still lead to chronic nicotine dependence.

Is Youth Nicotine Exposure Really Declining?

As a result, it is premature to declare victory; youth nicotine exposure may not be declining as rapidly as cigarette smoking rates alone suggest. Although nicotine remains the most common substance used in e-cigarettes, cannabis vaping has become progressively prevalent. Studies indicate that approximately 30% to more than 50% of adolescents who use e-cigarettes also report vaping cannabis or THC. Historically, cannabis–nicotine co-use primarily involved combustible products—cannabis and cigarettes. Increasingly, however, this combination occurs through noncombustible products, especially cannabis and nicotine vaping devices. Nicotine pouches represent a newer nicotine source that may further diversify patterns of co-use among youth.

This shift matters because cannabis/THC–nicotine co-use has emerged as an important psychiatric and public-health concern, particularly among adolescents and young adults. Although cannabis and tobacco have traditionally been studied separately, growing evidence suggests their combined use represents a potentially higher-risk pattern of substance exposure.

Health Risks Associated with Cannabis and Nicotine Co-Use

Co-use of cannabis and nicotine is associated with greater dependence liability, heavier substance use, cognitive impairment, cardiovascular and pulmonary injury, and growing evidence of adverse psychiatric outcomes. Both nicotine and THC may produce acute cardiovascular effects, including tachycardia, sympathetic activation, and blood-pressure changes, raising concerns that combined exposure may amplify cardiovascular risks.

Today's cannabis co-user is often combining nicotine with far more potent THC exposures than earlier generations experienced. THC concentrations in legal and illicit products are substantially higher, particularly in vape concentrates, where THC levels may exceed 70%-90%.

Prevalence of Concurrent Cannabis and Nicotine Use

article continues after advertisement

More than 16 million Americans report concurrent cannabis and tobacco use. Among regular cannabis users, nicotine is the most common co-occurring substance. Depending on the population studied, approximately one-half to two-thirds of regular cannabis users use nicotine. The highest rates occur among adolescents and young adults, the same developmental period associated with peak vulnerability to addiction, psychosis onset, and long-term neuropsychiatric consequences.

Unlike cigarettes, vaping devices and nicotine pouches can be used discreetly throughout the day in schools, workplaces, gyms, and social settings. This permits near-continuous nicotine exposure while creating opportunities to pair nicotine with cannabis. The rise of cannabis vaping further facilitates co-use because THC and nicotine can now be delivered through nearly identical devices in the same environments.

Nicotine and THC act through different receptor systems but converge on common reward circuitry. Evidence suggests the relationship is bidirectional: cannabis users are more likely to initiate nicotine use, while nicotine users may progress to regular cannabis consumption. Experimental studies indicate each substance may enhance the reinforcing effects of the other, helping explain why co-users demonstrate higher rates of dependence, heavier use patterns, and greater difficulty achieving sustained abstinence.

Psychiatric Consequences of Cannabis and Nicotine Co-Use

The psychiatric implications are difficult to ignore. Cannabis alone has been associated with increased risk of psychosis, particularly among adolescents, genetically susceptible individuals, and users of high-potency THC products. Emerging evidence suggests cannabis/THC plus nicotine use may further increase risks. In high-risk individuals, concurrent use has been associated with higher rates of transition to psychotic disorders.

A recent study by Heather Ward, MD, and colleagues in Nature Mental Health reported that heavy cannabis use combined with even light tobacco use nearly tripled the likelihood of developing psychosis among vulnerable individuals. Beyond psychosis, co-use has also been associated with higher rates of depressive and anxiety symptoms, addiction, and suicidality, although causality remains difficult to establish.

article continues after advertisement
The Nicotine Ecosystem
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

An important change has occurred in how young people think about cannabis. Over the past two decades, cannabis use has become increasingly normalized among adolescents. Even though most teens are not using marijuana every day, many now view it as relatively harmless. This shift in attitudes matters because when a substance is seen as safe, young people may be more willing to experiment with it, use it more frequently, or combine it with other substances such as nicotine. As a result, changing attitudes toward cannabis may play a role in the growing overlap between cannabis and nicotine use among today's youth.

Nicotine, however, has undergone a remarkable cultural rebranding. For decades, nicotine was associated with cigarettes, smoke, cancer, and chronic disease. Today, it increasingly appears in the form of sleek vaping devices and discreet oral nicotine pouches. In some online communities, nicotine is marketed less as a tobacco product and more as a performance-enhancing or productivity tool. Vaping products, nicotine pouches, and “clean nicotine” messaging have become associated with entrepreneurship, gaming culture, Silicon Valley, podcast culture, and self-optimization movements.

Celebrity culture has also contributed. Hip-hop stars popularized the co-use of cannabis and tobacco through the invention and proliferation of "blunts". Direct promotion of cigarettes is socially unacceptable, but indirect normalization of cannabis–nicotine co-use remains common through culture, music videos, social media, and cannabis-centered branding. Many younger users may not realize blunt wrappers contain tobacco and nicotine, creating dual-drug exposure even when the tobacco filler has been removed.

Nicotine is addictive, but is used in NRT and vapes as an effective aid to quitting smoking. However, it should not be used by people who do not already smoke. For established smokers, vaping devices and oral nicotine products may represent meaningful harm reduction. For young people who have never smoked cigarettes, there are only risks and no tobacco-related harm to reduce.

Challenges in Identifying and Screening for Cannabis and Nicotine Co-Use

The result is a cultural environment in which cannabis is increasingly perceived as benign, nicotine is increasingly marketed and viewed as modern and functional, and the combination of the two appears socially normal. That convergence may be more important than either trend alone.

article continues after advertisement

From a clinical perspective, the transition from cigarettes to vaping devices and nicotine pouches has made cannabis–nicotine co-use substantially more difficult to recognize. In most clinical settings, neither THC nor nicotine exposure is routinely confirmed through biological testing. Without urine testing for THC metabolites or cotinine, the primary nicotine biomarker, clinicians must rely on self-report, which often fails to capture the complexity of contemporary polysubstance use patterns.

As a result, cannabis–nicotine co-use may be far more prevalent than it appears. Obtaining accurate information about nicotine, THC, or cannabis use among adolescents is far more complicated than simply asking, “Do you use marijuana?” Some young people may answer no because they equate marijuana exclusively with smoking a joint and not recognize vaping THC, using concentrates, consuming edibles, dabbing, or cannabis-infused products as forms of marijuana use.

Similarly, patients who once would have identified themselves as smokers may now describe themselves as people who vape or use nicotine pouches and therefore fail to report nicotine use unless specifically asked. Without diagnosis, opportunities for early intervention, treatment, and evaluation for psychiatric morbidity may go undetected.

Screening for nicotine use history should include e-cigarettes, disposable vapes, refillable vaping devices, and nicotine pouches, especially among younger cannabis users. Concurrent withdrawal syndromes add additional complexity to assessment because symptoms such as anxiety, irritability, sleep disturbance, restlessness, and impaired concentration overlap substantially between nicotine and cannabis withdrawal.

The Evolving Profile of the Cannabis–Nicotine Co-User

The archetypal cannabis–tobacco co-user was once a young person smoking cigarettes and marijuana. Increasingly, that individual may instead be carrying a nicotine pouch, vaping nicotine throughout the day, and intermittently using high-potency THC products. The substances and devices have changed, but the pharmacologic and behavioral interaction between nicotine and THC remains. The addiction risks and psychiatric consequences have become less visible—and therefore easier to underestimate.

item.title: Compassion and Forgiveness in a Fractured World
item.description:
Resilience

Compassion and Forgiveness in a Fractured World

How to nurture compassion and forgiveness in ourselves, our family, and community.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • We are able to nurture compassion and forgiveness, even in fractured communities.
  • Skills help individuals understand their nervous systems, strengthen resilience, and manage stress.
  • Although trauma can spread through communities, resilience, compassion, and hope can spread too.

Compassion and Forgiveness Increase Through Nervous System Regulation

In a fractured world where social media and even some world leaders often model division rather than compassion, and where asking for forgiveness can seem increasingly rare, we may wonder how to nurture compassion and forgiveness. While these qualities are often viewed through spiritual or psychological lenses, emerging research suggests they may also arise from a regulated nervous system. Evidence from a recent study in Rwanda indicates that compassion and forgiveness may be strengthened when people restore a sense of safety, balance, and well-being within their own bodies.1

Human perceptions, emotions, and behaviors can be profoundly influenced by the state of their nervous systems. When individuals are overwhelmed by fear, chronic stress, or trauma, their ability to connect with others can become compromised. Survival responses such as fight, flight, or freeze (withdrawal) focus energy on self-protection. This is not a moral failing but a reflection of human biology (not pathology). Under conditions of threat, the nervous system prioritizes survival over connection.

This understanding has important implications for societies recovering from collective trauma. Communities affected by war, genocide, pandemics, political violence, natural disasters, or historical oppression often experience not only individual suffering but also fractured relationships, mistrust, and strained social bonds. The challenge becomes not only how to help individuals heal, but how to restore connections to family and the wider community.

My connection to Rwanda began in 2016 when I traveled to Tanzania to train a group of young Rwandans in the Community Resiliency Model (CRM). During our time together, our shared vision became clear: accessible tools that could help people understand the impact of trauma on the body and strengthen well-being in everyday life, to help people carrying the wounds of the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

The young Rwandans created the Rwandan Resiliency and Grounding Organization (RRGO), a grassroots initiative dedicated to bringing resilience-focused skills into their communities. Among those young leaders was Dr. Sam Habimana, who had recently completed his undergraduate degree in psychology from the University of Kigali. His passion for helping his country heal was evident. Alongside his colleagues, he began bringing CRM skills into rural communities where survivors and released perpetrators live side by side, often carrying profound emotional and relational wounds decades after the genocide.

For Habimana, this work raised important questions. Could a biologically-based intervention such as CRM contribute not only to individual well-being but also to broader social healing? Could skills that help regulate the nervous system foster compassion, forgiveness, and social cohesion in communities recovering from genocide?

Increases in Social Cohesion, Compassion and Forgiveness

Driven by these questions, Habimana pursued advanced studies in the United States, earning his doctorate in 2025. His scholarship contributed to one of the most significant studies conducted on CRM to date. His work was recognized internationally, including acknowledgment by the International Society for Traumatic Stress Studies (ISTSS), reflecting both the quality of the research and its relevance to the global trauma field.

The study examined the effects of CRM among genocide survivors, released perpetrators, and mixed groups composed of both survivors and perpetrators. Thirty years after the genocide, participants struggled with trauma, grief, mistrust, and disrupted social relationships. Yet following CRM training, researchers found significant improvements in social cohesion, compassion, forgiveness, and resilience across all groups.

Perhaps most remarkable was the finding that participants in mixed groups—in which survivors and released perpetrators learned together—demonstrated meaningful improvements in social functioning. The results suggested that collective healing can occur even among individuals whose histories are marked by profound suffering and division.

These findings suggest that helping individuals regulate their nervous systems may create physiological conditions that support some of humanity's most important capacities-compassion and forgiveness. Compassion and forgiveness become more accessible when chronic activation of the nervous system connected to fear and threat lessen. Social cohesion becomes more attainable when individuals experience greater safety within themselves and greater connection with others.

The implications extend far beyond Rwanda. Although cultures, languages, histories, and traditions differ, human beings share the same fundamental biological architecture. Whether we live in Rwanda, the United States, Haiti, Ukraine, Northern Ireland, or elsewhere, our nervous systems function according to the same basic principles. We all experience stress. We all experience threat. We all possess innate capacities to cultivate our well-being, healing and human connection.

This universality is particularly important at a time when the world faces unprecedented mental health challenges. Millions are living with the effects of trauma, violence, displacement, poverty, natural disasters, climate-related stress, and social fragmentation. At the same time, there are not enough mental health professionals to meet the growing demand for services.

Community-Based Approaches Promote Well-Being

The findings from Rwanda suggest that scalable, community-based approaches such as CRM can help address this gap. CRM is not intended to replace psychotherapy or specialized treatment. Rather, it offers practical wellness skills that can be shared through schools, healthcare systems, humanitarian organizations, workplaces, faith communities, and grassroots networks. These skills help individuals understand their nervous systems, strengthen resilience, and manage stress before problems become more severe.

Importantly, resilience-building programs work best when integrated with professional systems of care. Individuals requiring more intensive support can be referred to trained clinicians, while communities benefit from widespread access to preventive and restorative skills. This public health approach allows resilience-building and mental health services to work together in complementary ways.

The lessons emerging from Rwanda are about what becomes possible when individuals reconnect with the wisdom of their own bodies. The Rwanda study suggests that compassion, forgiveness, resilience, and social cohesion may also be strengthened when people learn skills that help regulate their nervous systems and restore a sense of balance and well-being.

The young Rwandans gathered in Tanzania with a vision for helping their country. Their efforts led to the creation of RRGO, the expansion of resilience-building programs throughout Rwanda, and research that is now informing the global conversation about trauma, healing, and social cohesion. Trauma can spread through communities, but resilience, compassion, and hope can as well.

item.title: An Exploration of Universal and Personal Truths
item.description:
Education

An Exploration of Universal and Personal Truths

All ideas, personal or universal, invite questions, scrutiny, and challenges.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Neither research nor opinions are exempt from analysis.
  • The willingness to accept feedback advances skills, learning, and knowledge.
  • The words “in my opinion” may encourage conversations. It also signals openness.
Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

The history of intellectual and social progress is, in many respects, a combined personal and collective journey of thoughts, beliefs, and actions, marked by questioning and challenges. Over the years, this ongoing quest for improvement has involved a mix of successes and mistakes. This consistent personal and social movement has shaped and advanced skills, learning, knowledge, and social circumstances.

However, even with this in place, these discussions were sometimes supported and sometimes opposed. And yet, these different points of view (occasionally, but not always) led to the realization that what had previously been accepted as true was, in fact, not true, thereby leading to a new belief. The crucial point to note here is that universal truths—whether discovered or not—exist, are absolute, and immutable, whereas "personal truths" are not.

Personal truths are opinions. Self-evidently, opinions have a place, and they may create opportunities for ideas to be exchanged and challenged. However, when the term “my personal truth” is applied to an opinion, it negatively affects the social dynamics of the situation (Boghossian, 2007; Habermas, 1990; Kant, 1781/1998; Korsgaard, 1996; Kuhn, 1999; Longino, 2020; Popper, 1963).

In social dynamics, the phrase “This is my personal truth” has become a modern barrier to questioning and challenges. The utterance “This is my personal truth” can be presented as if it confers “some kind of ‘special immunity’ from challenge,” as though the words “This is my personal truth” somehow elevate a personal belief beyond that of an opinion and beyond being challenged.

From a universal standpoint, an opinion—no matter how sincerely held—is never exempt from analysis. Likewise, any research‑based idea or claim is not immune from scrutiny. All points of view, whether academically supported or not, remain subject to ongoing consideration, questions, examination, and challenges.

Research across psychology and philosophy has long shown that refusing to allow beliefs to be questioned, which includes the process of feedback, undermines the very method that produced the Enlightenment and the Age of Reason (Ellis, 2001; Ellis & Dryden, 1997; Glasser, 1998, 2000; Habermas, 1990; Kunda, 1990; Pronin et al., 2004; Scanlon, 1982).

Feedback Is the Essence of Advancement

The willingness to accept feedback is the essence of advancing skills, learning, knowledge, and the potential for further intellectual development and higher-order reasoning. I first became aware of the importance of feedback with my parents, which was always ongoing. This helped me through all of my schooling.

This awareness of how important feedback was continued when, at the age of 16, I began my apprenticeship. This then continued when I began training in the Goju Karate style of Chojun Miyagi and Gogen Yamaguchi.

This ongoing attentiveness to feedback then continued during my 10 years as a tradesman. This also persisted when I began my two years of night school, while still working. The purpose of my night school studies was to advance my academic qualifications for entry to university, which was successful.

article continues after advertisement

With this successful entry into university, I was soon required to submit my first written assignment. When it came time for assessment, the lecturer informed me that my assignment was well written. However (and I remember this as if it were yesterday), the lecturer said: “For a first-year student, this is a strong and well-argued assignment; however, your essay is no more than a presentation of opinions.

“What you have failed to do is support your points of view with research. You will need to resubmit your assignment, with citations, within the next seven days for reassessment.”

The lecturer was direct and to the point. I was very pleased with how this feedback was presented; it had integrity.

Source: Free Fun Art / Pixabay

From an academic perspective, I immediately understood that a personal opinion—even if sincere—was insufficient. As my lecturer also informed me, regardless of how strong and well-argued the ideas were, they required justification and evidence.

There are no cognitive barriers or obstacles when you are searching for universal truths. Every intellectual door is open; the only requirement is to continue working. As Albert Einstein noted: “It's not that I'm so smart, it's just that I stay with problems longer.”

Clearly, importantly, and self-evidently, that’s the difference between working to discover universal truths and not working. It is the application of perseverance where insight and knowledge may arise. And knowledge changes when quantifiable evidence is located.

Crucially, the universal pursuit of knowledge is corrigible, i.e., capable of being continually corrected, improved, reformed, refined, and enhanced. Subsequently, for me, this first (opinion-based) university assignment, together with the lecturer's insightful feedback, has influenced and shaped my academic writing ever since.

Ideology

Associated with this, all of my years of university studies also introduced me to the concept of ideology. The research is unambiguous: Ideology resists correction; it ignores evidence, denies objective, universal truths, and places its own desires above universal reality. This is why ideology cannot and does not produce universal knowledge (Ecker et al., 2022; Harris, 2026; Rose et al., 2024).

Further to this, in terms of ideology, no matter how hard you work or what you say, the outcome and the ideology still remain in place. Consequently, skills, knowledge, and insight do not advance (Boghossian, 2007; Duvenhage, 2024; Haidt, 2001; Kant, 1781/1998; Korsgaard, 1996; Popper, 1963).

Within this broader context of ideology’s resistance to evidence, a modern linguistic expression has emerged, namely “my personal truth.” This phrase appears to function as an epistemic (i.e., knowledge-advancing) barrier (Boghossian, 2007; Duvenhage, 2024; Ellis, 2001; Ellis & Dryden, 1997; Haidt, 2001; Kunda, 1990; Popper, 1963; Pronin, Gilovich, & Ross, 2004).

article continues after advertisement

Consequently, the research also indicates that a personal truth is not a universal truth. A personal truth is an opinion—to which everyone is entitled—and, in terms of integrity, opinions are best expressed with the phrase “in my opinion.”

This—“in my opinion”—phrasing acknowledges that what is being expressed is a belief. The words “in my opinion” may also encourage further conversations. It also signals openness rather than defensiveness. And it keeps the path open for analysis, knowledge, and cooperative learning to take place (Boghossian, 2007; Duvenhage, 2024; Haidt, 2001; Korsgaard, 1996; Popper, 1963).

item.title: Could Chronic AI Use Lead to "AI Brain"?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Could Chronic AI Use Lead to "AI Brain"?

Can information technology directly injure the brain?

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • AI has already been associated with a range of negative findings, despite promising use-cases.
  • Early empirical research already shows neurobiological and psychosocial changes.
  • From "computational injury", improper AI use may lead to a syndromal clinical presentation in the near future.
  • A coherent research agenda is needed to study the impact of AI and guide best practices for AI use.

AI researchers (Tuckute et al., 2024) showed that a GPT-based encoding model could predict, and then deliberately drive or suppress, activation in human language networks —sentences the model rated as surprising and well-formed activated networks strongly, while bland, predictable text left them quiet. This study looked at suppression over a short timespan, but what happens from such suppression of language centers over time?

Like unused muscles, will brain areas atrophy and become permanently impaired? Negative neuroplastic effects—as contrasted with the beneficial impact of therapeutic agents on the brain, more familiar in discussions of neuroplasticity—could, if left unchecked, dominate over time and lead to irreversible impairment, particularly among those who overuse or misuse this powerful technology.

Take chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as a loose analogy—slow damage that accumulates in the brains of athletes from repeated head impacts, confirmable only at autopsy. Repeated injuries can add up to clinically significant damage—even smaller blows to the head once considered to be insignificant.

The story of CTE is a cautionary one. The carryover to AI is that we have chronic exposures already known to be toxic to a range of brain systems. Will we see "AI Brain" —a recognized AI-associated neuropsychiatric disorder, or AIAND—emerge as a clinical syndrome? What we don't know is what may happen over time. Selected potential mechanisms of injury, in this case "computational injury", are presented below, drawn from a growing body of research.

There are already findings on imaging suggestive of brain injury from AI. Geissler and colleagues (2023), using functional near-infrared spectroscopy, found reduced dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation when participants offloaded tasks to a digital assistant—a candidate neural substrate for the disuse pattern. Zheng and colleagues (2025), using diffusion tensor MRI, found that microstructural integrity of frontal white-matter tracts predicts how people use external memory aids—evidence that cognitive-offloading behavior has a structural brain signature, though correlational rather than causal.

Skill Decay and Automation Bias

Dratsch and colleagues (2023) found that very experienced radiologists' diagnostic accuracy fell from 82.3% to 45.5% in the presence of incorrect AI predictions; less experienced cohorts fared even worse. Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt's (2012) systematic review of 74 studies established automation bias—the tendency to over-rely on automated output, including accepting incorrect suggestions—as a common phenomenon mediated by user expertise, trust, and workload. Training and accountability were among the factors shown to reduce such bias. Along these lines, Abdulnour, Gin and Boscardin (2025), writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, describe a triad in medical training: deskilling, mis-skilling, and never-skilling. Further research is needed to see how much skill decay generalizes to other groups and different skill sets.

article continues after advertisement

Attachment Interference

Fang and colleagues (2025), in a four-week MIT/OpenAI RCT (currently a preprint), found that higher daily ChatGPT use predicted greater loneliness, emotional dependence, and less real-world socialization. Rubin and colleagues (2025), across nine experiments reported in Nature Human Behaviour, found identical responses rated as more supportive when participants were told they came from a human being, versus AI. Riva, Wiederhold and Mantovani (2024) argued that online interactions lack the more connected and embodied "we-mode"—behavioral synchrony, shared attention, interbrain coupling, emotional attunement.

While there is likely benefit from AI to offset the negative health effects of social isolation (De Freitas et al., 2026), without care to maintain and deepen the capacity for human connection, dependency on AI for connection could lead to long-term loss of basic attachment skills. Use of relational AI to substitute rather than augment human connection—despite the allure of a near-infallible digital buddy—could cause long-term damage to attachment systems, with future problems in relationships and relationship-related health outcomes.

Bias Amplification

Researchers (Glickman & Sharot, 2025), in a peer-reviewed series of experiments with more than 1,400 participants, showed that human-AI feedback loops amplify perceptual, emotional, and social biases significantly more than human-human interactions do—the amplification operating in part because users underestimate AI's influence on their own judgment. Such biases, if not corrected for, have the potential to snowball into problematic distortions in perception of oneself and others—leading to potential impairment in productivity and satisfaction in work and professional environments. We are already seeing such changes as a result of social media and a shift to online relationships.

AI could exacerbate the situation, and companion bots have already shown negative outcomes, especially in younger populations. According to Sun et al. (2026), while chatbots may have advantages, risks include "time displacement, psychological dependence, and unrealistic relationship expectations." These psychosocial factors ultimately can increase risk of mental illness, with potentially significant effects on the brain and body.

article continues after advertisement

Research Directions

Longer-term prospective studies looking at groups of people over time would go a long way to establish whether AI is causing brain damage in a syndromal constellation. The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948 and still running, followed thousands of Massachusetts residents over decades and established the concept of cardiovascular risk factors—smoking, hypertension, cholesterol levels, obesity—through prospective observation of an initially healthy population. As with other complex health problems, it is to be expected that AI could lead to a range of problems, compounded by the presence of multiple direct and indirect factors above and beyond the problematic effects of conventional information technology and online environments.

Despite the swelling risk, it is important to keep in mind the potential benefits of AI-based technologies. Understanding the risks and benefits of AI will help us identify how to best use it and avoid common problems. Such data would also inform future AI design to tip the balance toward augmentation rather than diminution. The framework presented here is intended as a concept to help organize and plan our approach to AI, rather than to define a clinical entity.

item.title: Raising Resilient Adolescent Girls in a Digital Culture
item.description:
Parenting

Raising Resilient Adolescent Girls in a Digital Culture

Prepared parents can help adolescent girls become emotionally strong.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Today’s digital culture poses unique challenges to the mental health of adolescent girls.
  • Adolescent girls still need affection, limits, role models, perspective, wisdom, and encouragement.
  • Effective parenting principles and skills improves the chances that adolescent girls will thrive.

This post is part of a series on adverse childhood experiences. Read the other parts here.

Parenting is challenging, especially for parents with their own hidden wounds from childhood. As a general rule, don’t compare yourself to others. You don’t have to be like anyone else. You have unique experiences and strengths that will reach your children like no one else can. Give yourself credit for the good you do. They don’t need perfection. They need you.

In their classic work, Reviving Ophelia, Pipher and Gilliam brilliantly capture the challenges for adolescent girls coming of age in today’s digital culture. Here are some of their suggestions for parents.

1. Relax and have fun, including times with and apart from the kids.

2. Don’t feel like a failure. Understand the challenges of adolescent girls’ developmental stage and today’s culture. Don’t be too hurt by their rejections as they test their limits. Be low-key and accepting, and they’ll likely talk with you.

3. Create a secure family environment, a comfort in their storms. As best as you can, focus on appreciation, encouragement, affection, commitment, time together, and spiritual well-being. Joy, humor, kindness, and trust go a long way. Model self-acceptance, including a relaxed feeling about your own appearance and kindness with your imperfections.

4. Recognize that your influence matters. For instance, fathers have great power to influence girls for good or bad. Wise fathers will avoid sexist jokes/cracks and suggestions that their worth is less than men’s. They can teach girls to change tires, throw a baseball, or build a patio. They can model good male/female relationships and teach them that it’s OK to be smart. They’ll be emotionally available. Such behaviors promote self-esteem and confidence in girls’ relationships with the opposite sex.

Parents can show their adolescent girls that they enjoy them, listen to them, and are appropriately involved in their lives (hovering, however, erodes self-confidence). Some parents hold comfortable one-on-one monthly chats with their children, where the children can ask anything they want. Parents can involve adolescent girls in what they do—exercising, cooking, building projects, planting trees, going out for ice cream. Positive parents will apologize for mistakes, limit comments on appearance, and greet their girls with a smile.

5. Set limits. The authors assert that the more time spent offline, the happier teenage girls are. Many adolescent girls can articulate the dangers of the digital culture, but can’t get off their devices. They need a firm but loving structure that says, “We love you and care enough to set limits,” which helps teens to become responsible, independent, and confident. Specifically, parents can:

article continues after advertisement
  • Limit social media time to 30-60 minutes a day, perhaps just before dinner. Then have them turn it off, telling friends that delayed responses are not personal, so no one feels singled out.
  • Don't allow girls to sleep with their phones. Sleep deprivation is linked to depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and self-harm. Encourage them to ask friends not to text or call after 10 p.m., so everyone understands the family rule and no one feels singled out.
  • Discuss rules, such as parents can inspect phones anytime, no sexy selfies, no phone in bed, phones are charged in the kitchen or locked up at night until after breakfast. Firm rules for younger children can become guidelines with teens, which are negotiated with respect and love.

6. Encourage real-life connection. Protect times for family interactions. Share hobbies and activities. Discuss the day as you prepare meals and drive to school. Place phones in a basket at mealtime. Teach siblings to love and enjoy each other.

Encourage teens to get out of the house and participate in activities requiring them to work and talk together, such as parties, cookouts, school activities, and hanging out with friends.

7. Teach girls to find contentment in wholesome pleasures, not drugs. These include nature, sports, exercise, arts, music, backpacking, reading, meditating, tuning engines, kind deeds, building character and self-respect, and keeping a gratitude journal.

Advanced parenting skills, to be described in a future post, can help parents help adolescent girls cope with particularly vexing challenges in today's digital culture.

item.title: Bridging the Acculturation Gap in Immigrant Homes
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Bridging the Acculturation Gap in Immigrant Homes

How immigrant families navigate culture, identity, and belonging together.

Posted June 9, 2026

Key points
  • Acculturation gaps grow quietly as children adapt faster than parents.
  • Language loss often weakens emotional closeness inside immigrant homes.
  • Code-switching can create identity strain and feelings of not belonging.
  • Honest communication and shared culture can turn distance into connection.

In most immigrant families, the distance between parents and children grows in quiet ways. It does not start with a fight. A child starts answering in English when spoken to in Mandarin or Spanish. A parent stops asking follow-up questions because the answers have started feeling foreign. The jokes stop translating, and certain topics become easier to avoid than to explain.

Researchers refer to this as the acculturation gap: the cultural and emotional distance that develops when immigrant children adapt to a new country more quickly than their parents do. Children move through the dominant culture every day. School, friendships, social media, and workplaces all pull them steadily toward new ways of thinking, communicating, and belonging. Parents tend to adapt more gradually, often staying more connected to the language, values, and social world they carried from home. Neither of those trajectories is a mistake. But over time, they begin to pull families in different directions, and the gap between them is rarely dramatic enough to trigger the alarm. It just quietly widens with one untranslated moment at a time.

Recognizing this process is not about blaming either generation. It is about taking on one of the most defining dynamics in immigrant family life, which touches millions of families, yet does not get enough honest attention.

When Children and Parents Adapt at Different Speeds

Acculturation is not something that happens to a family all at once. It happens to each person differently. The difference in pace is where a great deal of relational strain originates.

For children, adaptation is less a choice than a daily condition. The social codes of school, the humor of peers, and the unspoken rules of belonging influence children. Learning to navigate them quickly is often a matter of social survival. A child who cannot read the cultural cues of their classroom or neighborhood pays for that by feeling isolated. The learning happens fast because it has to.

Parents have a different perspective. Their social lives are often shaped by their ethnic community, workplace routines, or ongoing ties to their home country. Maintaining familiar values and practices is not stubbornness for many. It is what makes daily life feel coherent and stable in a country that otherwise feels uncertain or unfamiliar.

Both responses are reasonable. Research conducted with Chinese-American and Mexican-American families has found that wider acculturation gaps are linked to more family conflict, lower family cohesion, and higher rates of psychological distress in adolescents. What tends to look like disagreements about rules or expectations is usually something deeper. It is usually two people operating from increasingly different assumptions about how the world works and what they owe each other.

The Quiet Drift at Home

Here is what the gap looks like on an ordinary Tuesday evening. A teenager does not mention the friendship group that would take too long to explain. A parent senses something is being withheld but does not know how to ask. The conversation about the future stalls out because the two people having it are working from very different ideas about what a good future even means.

article continues after advertisement

Children in these families often begin self-editing long before anyone notices. They share less, not out of disrespect, but because of the emotional labor of translating. Their inner world starts to feel like more than the conversation is worth. Parents often interpret that withdrawal as distance or defiance, when it is more accurately described as exhaustion.

Career ambitions are a common fault line. A parent who spent years prioritizing stability in another country may struggle to understand a child who wants to pursue something uncertain. A child immersed in a culture of individual fulfillment may struggle to explain why security alone does not feel like enough. Both positions make sense in the given situation. But they rarely feel that way in the middle of an argument. Family love does not disappear in any of this. But the ease with which it gets expressed changes a lot. The warmth is still there, but it starts having to work harder to get through.

Identity Caught in the Middle

There is an internal version of the acculturation gap that is harder to talk about. It does not live between parent and child. It lives inside the child. Immigrant-origin children often become skilled at shifting between versions of themselves depending on context. One self for home, another for school, another for work. Code-switching becomes so automatic that it stops feeling like a conscious act. But automatic does not mean easy. It is tiring in a way that is difficult to articulate to people who have never had to do it.

Researchers use the term marginality to describe this in-between position: feeling too assimilated to belong fully in the heritage community and too ethnically marked to feel unreservedly at home in mainstream spaces. Some people eventually find something useful in that position. Having lived across cultures can produce a real flexibility, a capacity for empathy that others do not always develop. But for others, the experience settles into something more chronic: a low-grade feeling of not quite being from anywhere.

article continues after advertisement

Academic success or professional achievement does not fix this. When the acculturation gap goes unaddressed, it can produce a kind of internal fragmentation. That fragmentation can outlast whatever external markers of success a person accumulates. It is worth sitting with.

When the Gap Becomes a Bridge

Some families grow closer through this process. The research consistently shows that emotional closeness within the family is genuine warmth, not just proximity. Adolescents who feel genuinely supported at home tend to navigate identity tensions with more steadiness, even when the cultural disagreements remain real and unresolved.

A heritage language is not only a tool for communication, but it also carries humor, memory, and affection that often do not survive translation into English. Bilingualism matters in ways that go beyond the practical. When parents and children find ways to stay inside that shared linguistic space together, something important gets preserved. Families that treat the heritage language as a source of pride tend to maintain a kind of closeness that monolingual communication alone cannot replicate.

Storytelling is another underestimated resource. Parents share the experience of migration: the uncertainty, the cost, the cultural pride that kept them going. The children gain a way to locate themselves inside a larger family story. This kind of historical grounding changes what the gap feels like. Instead of being caught between two worlds with no clear connection to either, a child starts to understand themselves as part of a narrative that was already underway before they arrived.

Finding the Way Back to Each Other

Honesty starts to help them find their ways together. When families name openly that parent and child are navigating genuinely different cultural realities, shame lifts on both sides. A lot of what has been felt as ingratitude or failure turns out to be something more structural. Once that is understood, it becomes more forgivable.

article continues after advertisement

Language is one place where families can start. Creating intentional space for the heritage language at home matters not as an obligation but as something the family values together. Parents who approach their child’s world with genuine curiosity keep the door open longer. Children who let their parents in, even partially, often find the distance considerably more negotiable than silence made it appear.

Schools and community organizations can support these families, too, but only when the support is genuinely informed by immigrant family dynamics rather than applying a one-size-fits-all framework. Culturally sensitive counseling that acknowledges the acculturation gap directly, rather than treating it as a generic family communication problem, can make a real difference.

Conclusion

The acculturation gap is not evidence of a broken family. It is what happens when people are doing the hard work of building a life across two languages, two sets of values, and two very different ideas about what home means. It happens at the same time, usually without much outside acknowledgment.

When families can name that experience, the space between parent and child becomes something that can be worked on without silence. The gap may never close completely. With honesty and genuine effort on both sides, it can become the place where something new and more expansive gets built.
